title: Does hot sand make more girl sea turtles?
blurb: Warm sand makes turtle eggs hatch as girls. On warm beaches of the Great Barrier Reef, almost all young green turtles are now female.

cover.alt: Two tiny baby green sea turtles crawling across the sand towards the sea.

source.name: NOAA Fisheries
source.title: Rising Temperatures Turning Major Sea Turtle Population Female
source.authors: NOAA Fisheries Southwest Fisheries Science Center

original.title: Environmental Warming and Feminization of One of the Largest Sea Turtle Populations in the World
original.authors: Michael P. Jensen, Camryn D. Allen, Tomoharu Eguchi, Ian P. Bell and others, with Peter H. Dutton

cards.b: A mother sea turtle digs a hole in the beach and lays her eggs in the sand. The warmth of the sand decides whether each baby becomes a girl or a boy. Warmer sand makes more girls. Beaches are getting hotter as the Earth warms. So are fewer boy turtles being born now?

Michael Jensen of NOAA Fisheries in California led the study. NOAA is a US government agency that studies oceans and sea life. Camryn Allen of NOAA Fisheries in Hawaii worked out how to tell a turtle's sex from a blood test. Scientists from Queensland in Australia and from WWF-Australia joined them. They published in January 2018.

The team worked on Australia's Great Barrier Reef, where many green turtles feed. They caught hundreds of turtles of all ages, took a little blood, and let them go. Hormones, which are chemical messages in the blood, showed whether each turtle was female or male. Genes in the blood showed which beach each turtle had hatched on: the warmer north, or the cooler south.

img.alt: Green sea turtles resting at the edge of the water on a beach, with a small boat and a cloudy evening sky behind.
img.credit: NOAA Fisheries Southwest Fisheries Science Center (public domain)

cards.b: Turtles from the cooler southern beaches were about two-thirds female. Turtles from the warm northern beaches were almost all female: about 87 of every 100 adults, and 99 of every 100 young turtles. So for about 20 years, the northern beaches have made hardly any boys.

img.alt: A big adult green sea turtle on wet sand at the edge of a calm, blue sea.

cards.b: Hundreds of turtles were tested, and the blood test had been checked against other methods, so the numbers are strong. But this is one region. Scientists do not yet know how many males are needed to keep the group healthy. A few males can mate with many females, so the group may cope for a while.

About 200,000 female turtles nest on the northern beaches, one of the biggest groups of green turtles in the world. If almost no males hatch for many years, the group could shrink. People may need to cool some nests, for example with shade or water. India's olive ridley turtles, which nest in Odisha, also hatch as girls or boys depending on the warmth of the sand.

Is sand warmer in the sun or the shade? Fill two small bowls with sand, with a parent's help. Put one in a sunny spot and one in the shade for an hour. Then push a finger gently into each. Which feels warmer deep down? A turtle's eggs sit in sand like this, and its warmth decides if they hatch as girls or boys. That is why the spot a mother turtle picks matters.
cards.note: Touch the sand gently first, in case it is hot.

cards.b: Some people want to shade turtle nests or move eggs to cooler places, to make more boys. Others say we should not interfere with wild animals. Should people help the turtles this way? Or should we only try to stop the Earth from warming? What do you think?
